items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-24
items.q: I knew Charlie Parker and I didn't know Big Spider-Bank

ctx.x: Now, it's been said that, and I think Frank Power said this in a tape that he did in Bidebeck's life, that there was only one other musician that bare any resemblance to Bix Bidebeck. In the sense that both these musicians were victimized by the changing values of their time. And he mentions Charlie Parker. Now, I don't want to talk about, I don't want to bring up Charlie Parker. I'd rather talk about Bix Bidebeck. But, it's very interesting to me that he should bring up Charlie Parker in the relationship to Bix…

Well, it may have dramatized it to some extent, but I believe that the decline of the actualities behind the dream had already begun sometime earlier than that. I believe firmly that the American system has been in decline, demonstrably in decline, since the beginning of World War I. As far as the application of Charlie Parker, of course, I knew Charlie Parker and I didn't know Big Spider-Bank. However, it's fair to say that I know more about Big Spider-Bank than I know about Charlie Parker. In the first place,…
You don't understand the basis of his appeal?

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: I see clearly myself a relationship that goes, you know, from Bix to the moderns, the cool performers.

ctx.x: That worked certainly. Let's see. We were talking about recording sessions. It was Joe Maera- Mm-hm. He worked with him. Were you working for Joe Maera- Mm-hm.

Not really. What was the basis? No. Let me see what would I say was the basis. Joe, as you know, was very much interested in getting the music of New Orleans recorded. recorded. He has a feeling of commitment about it, the fact that there are a lot of musicians who hadn't been recorded or hadn't been recorded properly. And of course I felt the same way about it, and I always thought of myself as helping out, you know, in many cases proposing and producing sessions myself that I thought were suitable. And so there…
Yeah. Yeah, I'm just wondering how you fit Wiggs into something like this.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: my impression is that from listening, that Beiderbeck had a genuine love of melody.

ctx.x: Now, is there any comparison here to Beiderbeck, then?
I don't think so. I think that my impression is that from listening, that Beiderbeck had a genuine love of melody.
